reason: While the text does depict the conflict as national—presenting the Hebrew people (עַמִּי, בְּנֵ֣י יִשְׂרָאֵ֗ל) against Egypt and Pharaoh—the statement's claim that it is 'not depicted as personal or religious' is inaccurate. This passage is fundamentally religious in nature. It emphasizes God's covenant relationship with the patriarchs (אֱלֹהֵ֤י אֲבֹֽתֵיכֶם—'God of your fathers,' explicitly naming Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob), depicts God directly intervening to hear the cry of His people (שָׁמַ֙עְתִּי֙—'I have heard'), and frames the liberation explicitly for religious purposes (וְנִזְבְּחָ֖ה לַֽיהוָ֥ה אֱלֹהֵֽינוּ—'that we may sacrifice to the LORD our God'). The conflict is presented as both national AND religious, not exclusively national.
